While it is established that first-order logic augmented with fixed-point and least-fixed-point operators fails to fully characterize first-order queries executable in polynomial time, the question remains whether such a logic incorporating the minimum necessary features to define polynomial-time computable queries exists. This study examines the logical system $\mathrm{FO}(\mathrm{Count})$, which extends first-order logic with a counting predicate. We demonstrate that $\mathrm{FO}(\mathrm{Count})$ can express any query definable by a first-order formula combined with a $\mathrm{TC}^0$ circuit. Furthermore, we establish that $\mathrm{FO}(\mathrm{Count})$ is closed under first-order reductions and that its complete queries correspond to the complexity class $\mathrm{AC}^0\mathrm{L}$. These findings indicate that $\mathrm{FO}(\mathrm{Count})$ is a natural extension of first-order logic, offering a logic for $\mathrm{AC}^0\mathrm{L}$ that surpasses the expressive power of $\mathrm{FO}(\mathrm{Count})\oplus \mathrm{TC}^0$. Finally, we prove that $\mathrm{FO}(\mathrm{Count})$ cannot capture $\mathrm{NC}^1$ and does not suffice for the full set of polynomial-time computable first-order queries. Consequently, $\mathrm{FO}(\mathrm{Count})$ falls short of the requirements to resolve the logical characterization problem. The primary contribution of this work is the characterization of $\mathrm{FO}(\mathrm{Count})$'s complete queries as the language $\mathrm{AC}^0\mathrm{L}$, a result achieved through a novel method for characterizing the expressive power of $\mathrm{FO}(\mathrm{Count})$. This approach is expected to facilitate the analysis of other extensions of first-order logic. Additionally, we provide a new characterization of the complexity class $\mathrm{AC}^0\mathrm{L}$, which is significant in its own right. The paper concludes with a discussion of open problems. Our findings reveal a phase transition in the extreme eigenvalue statistics, accompanied by a corresponding shift in the central statistics of the spectrum. Specifically, the distribution of the largest eigenvalue shifts from the universal semicircle law to the Tracy-Widom-Gaudin (TGW) law, while the central eigenvalue distribution shifts from the semicircle law to the generalized Wigner-Dyson (GWD) distribution. This work provides a comprehensive analysis of the statistical characteristics of the largest eigenvalue for the specified model. It holds significance for understanding the statistical properties of non-Hermitian random matrices and has potential applications in various fields, including quantum chaos, statistical physics, and the analysis of complex networks. In contrast, the penalized MLE (P-MLE) offers a unique solution that is straightforward to compute. This paper demonstrates that the MLE and P-MLE share the same support. Furthermore, we establish that the P-MLE converges uniformly to the true density, whereas the MLE converges only in probability. Additionally, we present a practical algorithm for computing the P-MLE and derive its convergence rate. Finally, through simulations, we compare the performance of the MLE and P-MLE. The results indicate that the P-MLE is less sensitive to outliers than the MLE. Moreover, the P-MLE achieves a superior convergence rate compared to the nonparametric estimator proposed by Groeneveld and McCulloch (1983). Finally, we apply the P-MLE to real-world data to illustrate its effectiveness. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate that the P-MLE outperforms the MLE. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews existing literature on MLE and P-MLE, Section 3 presents our main results, Section 4 provides an application, and Section 5 offers a discussion. All proofs are included in the Appendix.

In this game, two participants, the Explorer and the Director, collaborate to locate a target set $T$ within a family $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of an $n$-element universe. The Explorer queries a set $E$ from $\mathcal{F}$ and receives a response indicating whether $T$ is contained within it. The Director's objective is to maximize the number of queries the Explorer needs to make, while the Explorer aims to minimize this count. A problem's Explorer-duality number is defined as the minimum number of queries required to guarantee finding $T$, assuming the Director plays optimally to prolong the game. This paper establishes that for the Explorer-Director problem on trees, the Explorer-duality number is $O(\log n)$, whereas for graphs with bounded treewidth, the number is $O(\sqrt{n})$. These findings are derived from a randomized strategy for the Explorer. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the Explorer-duality number of the Explorer-duality number remains bounded for graphs with bounded treewidth. This implies that the problem of determining the Explorer-duality number of the Explorer-duality number for graphs with bounded treewidth is strictly less complex than the problem of computing the Explorer-duality number itself. Additionally, the paper presents results regarding the complexity of the problem involving the maximum density of a graph's feedback vertex set. Finally, the authors provide a characterization of the Explorer-duality number for tree powers, which are graphs constructed from trees by adding edges between vertices at a distance of at most $k$. This characterization is based on a novel concept termed a "tree decomposition of order $k$." The work concludes by outlining several open questions and potential directions for future research. Our findings indicate that while the ensemble-averaged MSD scales as $t^{\alpha}$ with $0<\alpha<1$, the single-trajectory MSD exhibits a more intricate time dependence. We derive the probability distribution of the single-trajectory MSD and demonstrate that it decays algebraically as $P(\Delta\langle x^{2}\rangle,t)\sim(\Delta\langle x^{2}\rangle)^{-3/2}$ for large displacements. These results are validated through simulations of a fractional Brownian motion model. Additionally, we explore the implications of these findings for diffusion-controlled reactions within viscoelastic media. Our analysis reveals that the reaction rate is enhanced by a factor of $2^{\alpha}$ compared to the Smoluchowski rate, a finding that aligns with the scaling behavior of the first-passage time distribution. Consequently, our work elucidates the stochastic nature of diffusion in viscoelastic environments. Finally, we highlight the potential applications of these results in fields such as biophysics and nanotechnology. This study examines a novel approach to enhance the performance of floating oscillators by employing a non-linear restoring force. The research specifically analyzes a surface-floating, non-linearly restoring wave energy converter (floater-WEC) and compares its efficiency against a linearly restoring counterpart. The floater-WEC features a buoyant, flat, circular floating body with a diameter of 10 meters, a mass of 100,000 kg, and a restoring spring with a stiffness of 1.5 MN/m. The system is equipped with a submerged, fixed, rectangular caisson-type turbine with a width of 1.5 meters and a height of 1.0 meter. The floater-WEC is subjected to a regular wave field with a height of 0.5 meters and a period of 6 seconds. The study investigates the effects of varying spring pre-tension and damping coefficients on the device's performance. Results indicate that the non-linear floater-WEC outperforms the linear version, achieving a maximum power absorption of 10.5 kW, compared to 10.2 kW for the linear design. Furthermore, the non-linear design demonstrates superior robustness, evidenced by a lower root mean square (RMS) force of 1.2 kN compared to 1.6 kN for the linear system. The paper also includes a sensitivity analysis of the non-linear floater-WEC's performance and concludes with a brief discussion on potential future research directions. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that non-linear restoring forces can significantly improve the performance of floating wave energy converters. Future research should explore various configurations of non-linear floater-WECs to further optimize their capabilities. Additionally, the study suggests that non-linear restoring forces could be a valuable tool for designing floating devices capable of operating in deeper waters. The paper concludes by highlighting the potential of non-linear floater-WECs to advance the field of hydrokinetic energy harvesting. This study employs a kinetic theory grounded in the adjoint action expansion to derive these coefficients, specifically deriving the energy-momentum tensor and charge diffusion tensors for both equilibrium and near-equilibrium states. By incorporating the leading-order (leading order and next-to-leading order) strong coupling constant $\alpha_s$ corrections within the perturbative QCD framework, we determine the transport coefficients for a quark-gluon plasma featuring a finite number of massless quark flavors. These results are then utilized to analyze the dynamical properties of the plasma, including the ratio of the speed of sound squared to the product of energy density and temperature, shear and bulk viscosity, and entropy production. The calculations are conducted across two distinct regimes: the relaxation time approximation and the collision kernel. Our findings indicate that in the collision kernel regime, the transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma are significantly more sensitive to the strong coupling constant $\alpha_s$ than they are in the relaxation time approximation. Furthermore, we observe that the ratio of shear to bulk viscosity is greater than one, a result that aligns with previous research. Finally, we demonstrate that the dynamical properties of the quark-gluon plasma are highly dependent on the collision kernel. These insights are anticipated to enhance our understanding of the dynamical properties of the plasma produced in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, the methodology presented here can be readily extended to investigate the transport properties of other quantum many-body systems. This paper introduces a unified, parameterized evaluation framework that integrates the most prevalent strategies—call-by-name, call-by-value, and call-by-need—within a single framework. We demonstrate that this design is not merely convenient but also natural, as it emerges organically from the refinement of a call-by-name machine. Furthermore, we establish soundness and progress relative to a standard call-by-name machine. Our proposed machine is both modular and extensible, facilitating the easy addition of new features and strategies. Additionally, we show that our machine can be adapted to a dependent type theory featuring higher-order abstract syntax and elimination rules for inductive types, thereby generalizing the simply-typed lambda-calculus. Finally, we provide an implementation of our machine within the Coq proof assistant. This formalization is not only a rigorous verification of our results but also a standalone resource for studying the machine. To our knowledge, this specific machine has never previously been formalized in Coq. The resulting library is fully executable, enabling the generation of machine-code evaluators for various strategies, which can be validated against the OCaml compiler. We have also extended our machine to support first-order features, such as pattern matching, which are crucial for the formalization of programming language meta-theorems. This extension is achieved by incorporating a specific syntactic layer into the machine. We present both theoretical and practical results concerning this extension. , the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) is a critical subject for understanding the galaxy's formation and evolution. The Gaia mission has provided an unprecedented catalog of astrometric data for over 3 million LMC stars, revealing a complex internal structure. This study investigates the internal kinematics of the LMC by analyzing the spatial distribution of proper motions and radial velocities derived from the Gaia Data Release 2 (DR2). We identify a significant population of LMC stars exhibiting a coherent rotation of approximately 40 km/s around the line of sight, a motion previously unobserved. This rotation is primarily driven by the kinematics of the LMC's northern arm, which moves in the opposite direction to its southern arm. Additionally, we detect a distinct population of stars with a proper motion of roughly 10 km/s, which we attribute to the LMC's interaction with the Sagittarius (Sgr) dwarf galaxy. These findings offer new insights into the LMC's internal structure and its evolutionary history. The data and findings presented here will be essential for future research on the LMC. We observe that the system's evolution can be precisely mapped onto a 2D quantum spin Hall model, where the effective mass and spin-orbit coupling are modulated by the magnetic field. However, this network is inherently untrusted, as nodes may act maliciously, such as by withholding their partial results. Consequently, clients must verify the correctness of these partial outcomes. While prior research has addressed this issue for specific tasks like matrix multiplication, this paper extends the approach to a broad category of linear computations. We introduce a method that enables the reconstruction of a vector from a random selection of approximately $O(n/\log n)$ out of $n$ partial results. This efficiency is achieved by transmitting $O(\log n)$ redundant pieces of information for each vector element. The proposed solution relies on polynomial interpolation over finite fields, utilizing a random polynomial to map the client's input vector to the network nodes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach is optimal up to the $O(\log n)$ factor regarding the number of redundant pieces required. Finally, we illustrate how this method can be applied to matrix multiplication. Our results indicate that the computational overhead is minimal, with a reduction in communication of up to 50% compared to existing solutions. Additionally, the method is straightforward to implement and can be easily integrated with established matrix multiplication algorithms. To our knowledge, this is the first work to address the problem of decentralized computation outsourcing for linear computations. These explanations are typically generated for a single, fixed state, which limits their utility in practical applications. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel framework that integrates XRL into the training process of a multi-step policy. The fundamental theorem concerning positive monoids establishes that for any positive monoid $M$, the set $\{n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \mid n \notin M\}$ is finite, and the largest element $d$ among the excluded values satisfies $M \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}d$. This document introduces a formalization of this theorem in Coq, utilizing ideal theory to characterize positive monoids. Specifically, a positive monoid $M$ is defined as an ideal of the monoid $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$. The document further demonstrates that the ideal $I(M)$, consisting of all $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ such that $n+d \in M$ for some $d \in \mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}$, is principal, generated by an element $d$. Consequently, $M$ is contained within $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}d$. The paper includes proofs of these results and the accompanying theorem. Additionally, the section on applications presents a novel proof of the fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials by leveraging the formalized theorem. A key advantage of our approach is that it does not require prior knowledge of the players' perceived best responses. Instead, it relies on the assumption that players act optimally within the perceived strategy space. Consequently, this framework offers a valuable tool for analyzing security games where players' perceived strategies are constrained by their information structure. This task is difficult because sequential specifications fail to capture the required invariants for concurrent contexts, and data structure invariants are notoriously hard to identify. We propose a solution that leverages refinement and abstraction principles: we demonstrate that if an implementation refines a sequential specification via a specific abstraction, it becomes a valid concurrent implementation. To overcome the limitation that finding such an implementation directly is often intractable, we introduce a novel proof technique. This approach first derives a refinement proof for a naive concurrent version that violates the specification, then refines this naive version into one that adheres to the specification. We validate our approach by automatically generating concurrent linked list implementations from scratch. Our results show that while naive implementations fail to meet sequential specifications, our generated versions succeed. Furthermore, unlike manual proofs in existing literature, our generated concurrent implementations are provably lock-free, ensuring freedom from both deadlocks and livelocks. Additionally, our implementations outperform manually crafted solutions by requiring fewer locks and allocating less memory. These findings establish a foundation for future research aimed at automatically producing correct, lock-free concurrent implementations. The associated code and proofs are accessible at https://github.com/alexander-roscher/cds-spec.

**I. INTRODUCTION**

Thermodynamics is a cornerstone of physics, describing how energy and matter transform. While classical thermodynamics is a macroscopic theory, it has been extended to the stochastic level, where systems evolve through random transitions between states. This stochastic thermodynamics has enabled the calculation of thermodynamic quantities for small systems and the formulation of fluctuation theorems, which define the probability distributions of these quantities. These theorems are crucial for understanding the thermodynamic performance of stochastic systems, including heat engines.

However, most stochastic thermodynamic models do not explicitly account for the internal structure of the system's states. Instead, they represent the system as a set of states without detailing their internal composition. This simplification is problematic because coarse-graining—the process of grouping multiple microstates into a single mesoscopic state—can release significant energy, thereby drastically altering thermodynamic performance. For instance, a molecular motor could theoretically achieve 100% efficiency if the energy released from merging microstates is fully utilized.
